info.bio: Beastie Boys es un grupo musical neoyorquino fundado en 1979. Comenzaron tocando hardcore punk en sus primeros discos, pero más tarde comenzaron a experimentar como pioneros del hip hop y el rap, convirtiéndose en referencia fundamental de los mismos. También han editado discos basados en el funk y el jazz y es frecuente que en sus discos de hip hop incluyan algún momento de rock o punk o algún corte acústico. También son conocidas las actividades de Turntablism y de producción musical de sus miembros.

own_scenes.desc: Adam «Ad-Rock» Horovitz, Adam «MCA» Yauch y Mike D venían del hardcore punk del downtown; Rubin fue su primer DJ y, tras «Cooky Puss» (1983), los fichó para Def Jam: «Rock Hard» (1984). Llegaron con chándales Puma rojos queriendo ser Run-DMC; Simmons los vistió con vaqueros rotos y zapatillas sucias, su propio uniforme: «los rompemos negros y los cruzamos blancos». Abrieron la gira Like a Virgin de Madonna (1985), conquistaron al público del Apollo con Run-DMC y Licensed to Ill (1986), producido por Rubin, fue el primer disco de rap número 1 en Billboard. «(You Gotta) Fight for Your Right (to Party!)», hecha medio en broma, les llenó las primeras filas de universitarios borrachos que los espantaron.

scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Con la música negra popular muerta estéticamente, el alma del pueblo pasó al underground: un funk ruidoso, áspero y tenso, demasiado desesperado para la radio negra. Los breaks de DJ Kool Herc en las fiestas de barrio del Bronx, Jazzy Jay, Afrika Bambaataa, DJ Hollywood, Grandmaster Flash y Eddie Cheeba convirtieron la mezcla de discos en arte: los chavales dejaron las bandas por dos platos, el scratch y los breaks repetidos, un collage posmoderno de toda la música grabada sobre un ritmo funky. Sylvia Robinson grabó en 1979 «Rapper’s Delight» de la Sugarhill Gang y fichó a Grandmaster Flash and the Furious Five, cuya «The Message» (1982), con Melle Mel, dio voz a los sin voz como no se oía desde «What’s Going On»; siguieron «White Lines» o «New York, New York». Las cajas de ritmos dieron un funk industrial y minimalista (el bombo 808, «Five Minutes of Funk» de Whodini), y Run-D.M.C. («It’s Like That», «Rock Box», «King of Rock», «Walk This Way» con Aerosmith en Raising Hell, 1986) asaltó la radio rock, seguidos por los Beastie Boys.

scenes.name: Rap y hip hop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: A finales de los ochenta el «rockero» es una figura tan obsoleta como lo fue el cantante pop en 1956: tres revoluciones toman la música popular (el DJ como fuerza creativa, el hip hop y la fusión ciberpunk de industrial, metal y hardcore). En 1975 Kool Herc reinventa el breakbeat en el Bronx; el rap es una evolución del dub jamaicano. Sugar Hill Gang, Kurtis Blow, los «mensajes» de Grandmaster Flash, Afrika Bambaataa (el Leonardo del beatbox, inventor del «electro»), el tocadiscos como instrumento, Run-DMC, Tackhead, L.L. Cool J, Eric B & Rakim y Public Enemy (It Takes A Nation Of Millions, la obra maestra del hip hop). El gangsta rap (Schoolly D, NWA, Ice Cube, Dr Dre, 2Pac), Beastie Boys, las raperas (MC Lyte, Queen Latifah), De La Soul, A Tribe Called Quest, Cypress Hill; en Gran Bretaña, Art Of Noise.

podcast.title: Early Formation and Evolution (1981-2010s)
podcast.body: The Beastie Boys began in 1981 as a "goof" by three guys from well-to-do New York families, initially motivated by drinking beer and meeting women. Over three decades, they evolved from a hardcore punk band into esteemed members of the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, recognized as one of the most important acts of all time in two different genres, ultimately ceasing activity with the death of Adam Yauch. "When they finally had to call it quits when one of them died three decades later, they were esteemed members of the Rock and Wall Hall of Fame and considered to be one of the most important acts of all time in two different genres."

podcast.title: British Airways Lawsuit (1984)
podcast.body: The Beastie Boys sued British Airways after the airline allegedly used a sample from their song "Beastie Revolution" (likely referring to "Cookie Puss") in a worldwide commercial without permission. The band won a judgment for $40,000, which marked the first money they ever made from music. They used these funds to rent an apartment and rehearsal space at 99 Christie Street. "The Beastie Boys heard it in New York in the cinema, and sued British airways. It was the first money they ever made out of music."

podcast.title: British Controversy and False Stories (1987)
podcast.body: During their *Licensed to Ill* tour, the Beastie Boys faced severe criticism from British politicians, one of whom advocated for their ban from the UK, citing their stage antics such as inviting female audience members to dance in cages and the presence of a giant motorized inflatable penis. British tabloids targeted them, with one paper running a false story alleging the band laughed at and taunted dying children with terminal leukemia. Although some of the affected children later defended the band, the damage to their reputation had already been done. "The British tabloids really had it out for them. One went so far as to carry a false story about the band laughing and taunting a group of dying children, kids with terminal leukemia."

podcast.title: "Sabotage" Music Video (1994) – 70s Crime Show Parody
podcast.body: The music video for "Sabotage" was directed by Spike Jonze, who had previously photographed skateboarders, and featured a concept devised by the Beastie Boys themselves. It parodied 1970s crime shows, complete with all the clichés and "bad moustaches." The video was shot with a skeleton crew, fitting everyone into one van, and without permits, allowing for quick filming on the streets of Los Angeles with a relatively tiny budget compared to other videos of the era. "The Beastie Boys came up with the concept that parodied 70's crime shows, complete with all the clichés and bad moustaches."

xref.title: Move to Los Angeles and Studio Construction (G-Sun)
xref.body: The band moved to Los Angeles and used profits from "License to Ill" to build their own studio, G-Sun, in the Atwater Village area (3218 1/2 Glendale Boulevard). The name "G-Sun" originated from a plumbing store next door, Gilson's, which had lost the "I" and "L" from its sign, leading owners to place a hyphen between the "G" and "S-O-N." The studio also served as their business office, private skate park, and home basketball court, with rent less than $1,500 a month. "The Beastie Boys moved to LA. xref.title: Paul's Boutique Album Artwork Location
xref.body: The iconic panoramic album cover for the Beastie Boys' 1989 album *Paul's Boutique* was shot at the corner of Ludlow and Rivington streets (99 Rivington) on the Lower East Side of Manhattan. The original Paul's Boutique store that inspired the album's name was out of business, so a sign was created and hung over Leigh Sportswear for photographer Jeremy Chutan's shoot. After the album gained fame, the sportswear store was replaced by a restaurant also named Paul's Boutique, which operated until 1997 when it became The Three Monkeys. A fire in January 2011 destroyed the building, leaving little to see today. "If you want to make a pilgrimage to where the building used to stand, it's at 99 Rivington in Manhattan."
